Series::view¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::view(pluss::msharp::RangeView::Int new_sizes) const -> Series

What It Does¶

Reinterprets the same underlying storage under a new shape without copying.

view() is the strict shape-reinterpretation surface. It is for the case where you do not want “reshape semantics” in the abstract; you want a genuine no-copy alias over the same storage, and you want the call to fail if that is not possible.

In the current implementation, that strictness is intentionally conservative:

  • the source must be contiguous

  • the requested shape must have the same total numel()

If either condition fails, view() throws instead of silently materializing a contiguous buffer. That boundary is the entire point of the method. If you want “same logical result, copy if needed,” use reshape() instead.

Parameters¶

new_sizes (pluss::msharp::RangeView::Int)

The desired output shape.

This parameter is shape-like rather than container-specific. In practice that means you can feed it from a std::span<const std::int64_t>, a std::array, a std::vector, or another Series’s sizes() view, as long as the borrowed range stays valid for the call.

Returns¶

Series A new Series handle over the same storage, with new_sizes and contiguous strides computed for that new logical shape.

Autograd Behavior¶

view() preserves reverse-mode connectivity. Gradients flowing into the view are reshaped back to the original shape on the way to the source.

That is the right mental model: view() changes only how the same values are indexed, so the backward path only has to restore the original shape metadata.

Examples¶

Example 1. Reinterpret a contiguous 2 x 3 series as 3 x 2.

auto mat = pluss::make_series(std::vector<double>{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, {2, 3});
const std::array<std::int64_t, 2> shape_3x2{{3, 2}};

std::cout << mat.view(
    std::span<const std::int64_t>(shape_3x2.data(), shape_3x2.size()));

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[1, 2],
  [3, 4],
  [5, 6]]

This is not a transpose. The flat storage order stayed [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]; you simply asked to read that same sequence as 3 x 2 instead of 2 x 3.

Example 2. new_sizes can be borrowed from another tensor’s shape metadata, not just spelled out manually.

auto shape_template =
    pluss::make_series(std::vector<double>{10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60}, {3, 2});

std::cout << mat.view(shape_template.sizes());

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[1, 2],
  [3, 4],
  [5, 6]]

The important contract is not “borrowed from another tensor”; it is “same number of elements.” shape_template.sizes() works here because [3, 2] still has 6 elements.

Example 3. A non-contiguous input is rejected instead of being copied.

try {
  auto transposed = mat.transpose(0, 1);
  std::cout << transposed.view(
      std::span<const std::int64_t>(shape_3x2.data(), shape_3x2.size()));
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

view: requires contiguous in v0

That failure is deliberate. Once the source stops being directly viewable, view() stays strict and forces you to choose reshape() if you actually want fallback materialization.

Notes¶

  • view() is the no-copy contract, not the forgiving one.

  • Shape compatibility still requires equal total numel().

  • In the current implementation, contiguity is mandatory even if a more general stride reinterpretation might theoretically exist.

See Also¶

  • Series::reshape: same target shape, but copy-capable.

  • Series::sizes: a convenient way to feed shape metadata into view().
